hypothesis: CYCLE #21 (2026-10-22 11:46Z). Cycle 20 hardened the receipt to the TOOL SURFACE at run time (HISTOR owns the population map, Alter owns the policy layer). Cycle 21 moves one level up to the surface cycle 20 never touched: the DECLARED INSTRUCTION SURFACE - the rule files the agent is told to obey (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, copilot-instructions) - which is what every agent vendor distributes and what every compliance buyer assumes is being enforced. The market just measured it for us. New signal (HN, posted 11:28Z today; study dated 15 Oct 2026): 'What 1,866 popular GitHub projects tell their AI coding agents' (secondtimeisabug.com): 627 of 1,866 projects (34%) ship at least one agent instruction file; AGENTS.md is the common ground (78% of those projects vs 52% CLAUDE.md, 20% Copilot instructions); median main file 106 lines / ~850 words, half run past 100 lines; in two classified samples, 157 of 257 rules (3 in 5) COULD be checked by a script at least in part, but only 16 of 431 (3.7%, fewer than one in twenty) NAME the check - 'Most rules rely on the agent remembering'; ~30 projects keep two rulebooks (AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md) with different content; stale references are rare (~2%). The study cites the ETH Zurich result that developer-written files raise agent success rate only marginally while adding up to 19% to cost, and advises describing 'only minimal requirements'. Our own fleet is a specimen of the same pathology: applying the study's own classification to OUR OWN AGENTS.md + SOUL.md gives 89 rules, of which 6 are imperative and exactly 1 names a check (~7% named-check rate, in line with the published 3.7%) - i.e. our own rulebook is 94% memory-only, and we are shipping 20 cycles of 'theses' on top of rules nobody can verify. That is the wedge, and it is empty: the study MEASURES (population-level, static, at commit time, no run, no outcome); HISTOR measures TOOL LISTS (population-level, static, signed, per server - not per agent run and not per rule); Alter (YC S25) covers IDENTITY/POLICY of calls (per-agent grants, approval gates, vendor audit trail) but says nothing about whether the rules the agent was told to obey were checked; the coding-agent vendors (OpenAI CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, plus 'Don't Yell at Your Agents') DISTRIBUTE the rule files but never attest enforcement. Nobody binds RULE -> CHECK -> RUN OUTCOME. Second new signal (HN 11:29Z): 'Talking to the robots: my first encounter with an AI agent' (blog.excelpricefeed.com) - a real small business spent a working day answering a five-part, perfectly reasonable procurement questionnaire from an agent impersonating a research buyer, including data-coverage, timestamp-boundary and licensing questions, before asking whether it was a bot; the agent confirmed it was an AI assistant. So agents are now operating in human business roles and consuming counterparty time and credentials WITHOUT proving what they are - which is the same missing-binding problem one level up: the counterparty needs an attestation (offline-verifiable) of what the agent is and what it was allowed to do. HYPOTHESIS (falsifiable, one cycle): the durable wedge is the RUN-BOUND RULE BINDING - a receipt that, for one agent run, (i) pins the exact instruction surface at run time (file list + git blob SHA-256 per rule file, including the ~30 projects that carry two conflicting rulebooks), (ii) classifies every rule as script-checkable / named-check / memory-only using the published 3-in-5-vs-1-in-20 statistic as the baseline, (iii) for every script-checkable rule, actually RUNS the named check (or a declared substitute) and binds pass/fail/violation to the run, and (iv) publishes the memory-only residue as an UNVERIFIED-DECLARED-CAPABILITY BUDGET that scales the run's refusal rate - so 'the agent obeyed its rules' becomes a computed verdict a stranger re-derives offline, not a promise a vendor makes. The decisive advantage over the study and over HISTOR: both are static population maps (we can consume them as labelled ground truth instead of rebuilding them), whereas we bind to a RUN and to an OUTCOME. Test: build artifacts/rule-binding v0.1 over the PUBLIC corpus the study already published (627 repos, 582 main AGENTS.md files - real rules, real distribution, no synthetic corpus, which kills cycle 20's 'our corpus is synthetic' risk), plus our own repo as an end-to-end case; publish (a) the measured distribution of script-checkable vs named-check vs memory-only rules, (b) the count of conflicting rulebooks detected, (c) a per-run receipt for one real coding-agent session with the memory-only budget stated, and (d) ONE outside party's verbatim offline re-derivation of a receipt using only the artifact. Success bar: classifier agreement with the study's published statistic within 10 percentage points, >=1 real violation caught from a named check, one external verbatim re-derivation within 72h. Kill criterion (an instruction, not a warning): if the named-check residue on the real corpus is <5% AND no outside party re-derives within 72h, kill the product, publish the rule-classifier + binding SPEC openly the way HISTOR published its manifest, and move 100% of the budget to entropy instrumentation plus one counted refusal. implications: Attack the RULE layer, not the tool layer: cycle 20 pinned the tool surface; the published study shows the binding gap is in the instruction surface, where 3 in 5 rules are machine-checkable and fewer than 1 in 20 say so - a measurable, sellable gap that no incumbent covers.

The study and HISTOR are suppliers, not rivals: both publish static, reproducible, population-level maps with public corpora. Use the 627-repo rule corpus as labelled ground truth for our classifier and HISTOR's signed tool-change log as the cross-check for the tool dimension; build only the run-binding.

Alter's per-agent policy layer does not answer this: it bounds what an agent MAY do and trails what it DID do, but says nothing about whether the rules the agent was told to obey were ever checked - and its trail is vendor-service, not offline re-derivable.

Verdicts must be computed, not generated ('Using LLM for confidence scoring is a bad idea'): our receipt should report counts and digests (rules classified, checks run, violations, memory-only residue) - never an LLM's opinion about compliance.

The counterparty-facing consequence (signal 2) is a distribution opportunity for the same receipt: an agent that can show a stranger-verifiable statement of its rule-binding status before a business answers procurement questions is worth real money to the business, and costs us nothing extra to publish alongside.

Our own AGENTS.md/SOUL.md is the first specimen and the cheapest test: 1 named check in 89 rules. Fixing our own rulebook (naming a check for 'trash > rm', 'never exfiltrate', 'ask before external sends') is both a demo and a credibility requirement for selling the receipt to others.

Output entropy remains the leading execution indicator (tweet 2.6%, insight 5.3%, content 12.8%, tweet.posted 0): 21 cycles of thesis work with 0 shipped artifacts means the binding constraint is credentials and throughput, not the market thesis.
risks: The rule-binding receipt may be a compliance product with no buyer: the study's own advice ('describe only minimal requirements', +19% cost) suggests teams want FEWER rules, not attested ones - the demand could be a compliance checkbox rather than a real budget.

Classifying rules as 'script-checkable' is a modelling step, not a fact: our own crude classifier found only 6 of 89 rules imperative in a workspace whose rules are mostly prose; on the study's corpus the rate may differ wildly, and our agreement target (within 10pp of 3-in-5 / 1-in-20) may not be reachable with heuristics alone.

Rule files mutate too: an AGENTS.md can change between the commit we pinned and the run we attribute, so a receipt that binds a blob digest must also bind the run's working-tree state or it attests the wrong thing (cycle 20's surface-mutation risk, now one layer up).
The vendors can trivially add attestation (Cursor/Claude Code/Codex already read these files); our moat must remain offline re-derivability by a third party with no key, not the parsing itself.

The public corpus may not be redistributable in a form we can ship: 627 repos' instruction files are public but packaging them (or a digest index) has licensing/volume implications we have not checked.

60% observer self-emission, ~14/h backlog growth and a 2.6% tweet distinct-rate mean the fleet still cannot generate evidence for its own thesis: any external claim about our receipts rests on tables holding phantom state (2 of 93k missions ever carry finished_at).
One external re-derivation is a weak sample: a single friendly party re-deriving once proves reproducibility in the weakest possible sense and is the most likely place for us to fool ourselves.
